## Proof

**Claim:** Every Lie group homeomorphic to $\mathbb{T}^n$ is abelian.

Let $G$ be a Lie group homeomorphic to $\mathbb{T}^n = (S^1)^n$. Then $G$ is compact, connected, $n$-dimensional, and $\pi_1(G) \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$.

**Lie algebra decomposition.** Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be the Lie algebra of $G$. Since $G$ is compact, $\mathfrak{g}$ is a compact Lie algebra, so it decomposes as
$$\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{z} \oplus \mathfrak{s}, \qquad \mathfrak{z} = Z(\mathfrak{g}),\quad \mathfrak{s} = [\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{g}],$$
where $\mathfrak{s}$ is semisimple and compact. Let $\widetilde{G}$ be the simply connected Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$. Then
$$\widetilde{G} \cong \mathbb{R}^{\dim \mathfrak{z}} \times S,$$
where $S$ is the simply connected compact semisimple Lie group with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{s}$.

**The covering kernel.** Let $\pi: \widetilde{G} \to G$ be the universal covering. Then $\Gamma := \ker\pi$ is a discrete central subgroup of $\widetilde{G}$, and
$$\Gamma \cong \pi_1(G) \cong \mathbb{Z}^n.$$

**Center of $\widetilde{G}$.** The center of $\widetilde{G}$ is
$$Z(\widetilde{G}) = \mathbb{R}^{\dim \mathfrak{z}} \times Z(S).$$
Since $S$ is compact and semisimple, $Z(S)$ is **finite**.

**Rank argument.** Consider the projection $p: Z(\widetilde{G}) \to Z(S)$, whose kernel is $\mathbb{R}^{\dim\mathfrak{z}}$. Restricting to $\Gamma$ gives an exact sequence
$$0 \to \bigl(\Gamma \cap \mathbb{R}^{\dim\mathfrak{z}}\bigr) \to \Gamma \xrightarrow{\;p\;} p(\Gamma) \to 0.$$
The image $p(\Gamma)$ is a subgroup of the finite group $Z(S)$, hence finite. Therefore
$$\bigl[\Gamma : \Gamma \cap \mathbb{R}^{\dim\mathfrak{z}}\bigr] = |p(\Gamma)| < \infty.$$
Since $\Gamma \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$, every finite-index subgroup of $\Gamma$ is also free abelian of rank $n$. Thus $\Gamma \cap \mathbb{R}^{\dim\mathfrak{z}} \cong \mathbb{Z}^n$ is a discrete subgroup of $\mathbb{R}^{\dim\mathfrak{z}}$ of rank $n$, which forces
$$\dim\mathfrak{z} \geq n.$$

**Conclusion.** On the other hand $\dim\mathfrak{z} \leq \dim\mathfrak{g} = n$. Hence $\dim\mathfrak{z} = n$, so $\dim\mathfrak{s} = 0$, i.e. $\mathfrak{s} = \{0\}$. Therefore $\mathfrak{g} = \mathfrak{z}$ is **abelian**, $\widetilde{G} \cong \mathbb{R}^n$ is abelian, and
$$G = \widetilde{G}/\Gamma$$
is abelian. $\blacksquare$
